name: Authors and Communicators
blurb: Writers, journalists, and educators explaining AI publicly.

members.hook: Ng did more than any single figure to turn machine learning from a graduate-school subject into a skill anyone could learn online, while simultaneously building the industrial-scale infrastructure, Google Brain among it, that made deep learning practical at big-tech scale.
members.name: Andrew Ng
members.moniker: AI Educator and Deep Learning Pioneer

members.hook: Brynjolfsson has spent three decades building the empirical case for how digital technology, and now AI, actually changes productivity and jobs, work that shifted from academic papers to boardroom strategy as generative AI forced every company to ask the same question he had been measuring for years.
members.name: Erik Brynjolfsson
members.moniker: Economist of the Second Machine Age

members.hook: O'Reilly has spent four decades doing the same thing under different names: spotting a technology shift before the industry has language for it, then naming it. 'Open source' and 'Web 2.0' both trace to conferences he convened, and his publishing house has been the technical-literacy backbone for the programmers who built the modern internet, and now AI.
members.name: Tim O'Reilly
members.moniker: Publisher Who Named Web 2.0 and the Open Source Movement

reading.body:
The three people in this category share a specific function: each made a technical domain legible to a broader audience at a moment when that mattered for adoption.

Andrew Ng's contribution sits at the intersection of education and infrastructure. He lowered the barrier to learning machine learning while also building the large-scale compute environments, Google Brain among them, that gave deep learning its industrial footing. The educational and the infrastructural work were not separate projects; each reinforced the other. Erik Brynjolfsson brought a different discipline to bear, constructing an empirical record over three decades of how digital technology actually moves through economies and labor markets. His work predates the current generative AI moment, which means it offers measured baselines rather than speculation. Tim O'Reilly's pattern across four decades has been terminological: he identified and named shifts, including open source and Web 2.0, early enough that the names shaped how practitioners organized around the underlying changes.

What the data does not cover is influence in any quantified sense, institutional affiliations beyond the hooks provided, or how these figures connect to the compute and power constraints that govern AI scaling today. The category is defined as communication and education, and the data stays within that boundary. Three people is a small sample, and the page does not claim otherwise.
